summary: Discovery focused on an air-gapped, on-prem deployment for regulated drug discovery workloads. Key concerns: offline updates, hardware/driver constraints, KMS/HSM integration, SSO and audit logs, and performance tradeoffs between Dedicated and private on-prem. Agreed next steps: share runbook, schedule benchmarks, and provide pilot pricing.
transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everybody thanks for hopping on, quick intros -- I'm Lena, AE on the life sciences vertical at Redwood. Carlos is our SE, Ava is solutions.
[00:12] Dr. Mira Patel: Hi, Mira here. Thanks for doing this. We're trying to understand if Redwood can run in our air-gapped environment for a drug screen NLP workload.
[00:20] Carlos Mendes: Great thanks Mira. Can you describe your infra and the regulatory constraints?
[00:28] Jonah Reed: Sure. We run a hardened on-prem cluster, no egress allowed from the subnet that hosts PHI or proprietary assay data. We have a discrete staging subnet that sometimes has controlled egress for updates, but policy leans toward manual offline updates, so tools need to support air-gapped install flows.
[00:47] Ava Zhou: Understood. Redwood supports a private deployment mode intended for VPC/on-prem. We have an air-gapped install procedure where images, packages, and model artifacts are bundled and transferred via secure media. It does require a short maintenance window for model pushes.
[01:05] Sofie Grant: Important: from compliance side we need proof of KMS/HSM integration, audit logs retention for 7 years, SSO/SAML and RBAC controls. Also a signed DPA and clarity on who holds keys.
[01:18] Lena Park: Yes, we can integrate with customer-managed KMS or HSM; keys stay on your side. We'll share the integration doc. Audit logs and exports are supported; retention windows can be configured but we'd like to align on what is local versus shipped to a control plane. For air-gapped, control plane connectivity is optional — we can run with a customer-managed control plane.
[01:38] Dr. Mira Patel: That last bit is critical. We can't have any telemetry leaving our network unless it's explicitly permitted. How are software updates handled?
[01:46] Carlos Mendes: Two main patterns: 1) Offline bundle — we package the runtime, Docker images or tarballs, model weights (or encrypted model shards) and a signed manifest. Elysian would pull these artifacts via removable media into a staging host and kick off an automated installer. 2) Staged gateway — a restricted gateway that we coordinate with your security team for limited, auditable egress windows. Both have pros/cons.
[02:09] Jonah Reed: For us, offline bundles are preferable. But we run mixed GPU types: a set of H100s for throughput, some older A100s, and a few inference-class cards. Drivers and CUDA versions are heavily curated by infra; we can't inject arbitrary kernel modules. How tolerant is Redwood to heterogenous hardware?
[02:29] Carlos Mendes: Runtime selects kernels based on architecture and sequence length; we support H100 and A100 families. For really old inference-only cards there may be perf differences, and on some configs we recommend quantized model variants. We'll need your exact driver/CUDA versions to map to supported runtime kernels. The onprem matrix we'll send asks for GPU make/model, driver, OS, and container runtime.
[02:52] Dr. Mira Patel: Another question: model weights — can we bring our own models? We have several fine-tuned models and some non-open weights that never leave our network.
[03:01] Ava Zhou: Absolutely. Private deployments allow customer-hosted model weights. The offline bundle can include encrypted model artifacts that Redwood signs for integrity checks. No model material needs to go to Redwood hosted control plane.
[03:12] Sofie Grant: About encryption — we require AES-256 at rest and in-transit, plus HSM-backed key wrapping for production keys. Any logs that might include tokenized PHI must be redacted or remain in the customer's ELK.
[03:26] Carlos Mendes: We support AES-256 at rest and TLS 1.2/1.3 in transit. For HSM, we have an integration pattern (PKCS#11 or cloud HSM options) and can operate with customer-managed keys. For logs, we can configure local logging endpoints and disable remote retention. We'll put that in the security doc.
[03:41] Jonah Reed: Performance — we expect sub-200ms for short prompts (<256 tokens) in some interactive tools. Is that realistic on an on-prem private deployment?
[03:50] Carlos Mendes: On H100 clusters yes, you can get sub-200ms for small seqs with right batching and KV cache warm. But air-gapped and CPU constraints can increase latency. If you need consistent low-latency at scale, Dedicated reserved capacity (Redwood-managed on your hardware or isolated pools) or a hybrid routing approach is an option. There is a tradeoff: lower latency often means more reserved capacity and higher unit cost.
[04:15] Dr. Mira Patel: We also need to know about model rollouts and versioning. How do you handle canary/rollback in an offline environment?
[04:22] Ava Zhou: Our deployment abstraction supports pinned model versions. For air-gapped flow we recommend a controlled rollout: push the new model to a staging cluster, run a subset of traffic via internal routing, and validate metrics locally. Rollback is simply re-pin to previous model version; the runtime manages KV cache invalidation. This does assume you keep prior versions available in your artifact storage.
[04:43] Lena Park: Quick question from sales perspective: what's your timeline and success criteria for a pilot?
[04:48] Dr. Mira Patel: Timeline is Q3 — pilot in July. Success criteria: 1) no egress for data, 2) integration with our KMS/HSM and SSO, 3) throughput targets for our batch inferencing jobs, and 4) documented runbook for offline updates.
[05:04] Jonah Reed: Also cost targets — we can't exceed our infra OPEX budgets, so we need realistic numbers comparing keeping everything fully on-prem vs Redwood-managed Dedicated nodes.
[05:13] Carlos Mendes: We'll prepare a pilot proposal with two scopes: pure on-prem private deployment and a Dedicated hybrid (Redwood-managed isolated pool connected via private link during restricted windows). We'll include cost comparisons and perf expectations.
[05:25] Sofie Grant: One more — can you supply an NDA and your standard DPA? Legal will review before any pilot.
[05:31] Lena Park: Yes we'll attach NDA and DPA templates.
[05:34] Dr. Mira Patel: Any notable limitations we should be aware of?
[05:37] Carlos Mendes: A few practical notes: 1) Some open-source model optimizations assume newer CUDA toolchains; if your infra is older, quantization and smaller model variants may be recommended. 2) Offline update cadence adds operational overhead for model rollouts. 3) If you use extremely tight FIPS-only stacks, we may need a short compatibility project.
[05:59] Jonah Reed: That FIPS point matters. We'll flag it in the infra inventory.
[06:03] Lena Park: Great. We'll follow up with the onprem sizing matrix, the air-gapped runbook, SOC2/ISO summary, and proposed pilot scopes. Any other questions?
[06:12] Dr. Mira Patel: Not right now. Appreciate the clarity.
[06:15] Sofie Grant: Thanks all.
[06:17] Lena Park: Thanks everyone. Recap: Redwood to share docs and propose pilot; customer to provide infra inventory and compliance boundary. We'll schedule the benchmark window in two weeks.
[06:26] [crosstalk] Notes: minor transcription errors possible, speaker overlaps near end.
